canberra.title: Taylor reignites public service wars with tirade against ‘wasteful bureaucracy’
canberra.snippet: Canberra public servants again face the threat of the Coalition taking an axe to the public service after Opposition Leader Angus Taylor ...
canberra.content:
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor says areas of the public service could “go immediately” if the Coalition won the next federal election. Photo: Facebook.

Canberra public servants again face the threat of the Coalition taking an axe to the public service after Opposition Leader Angus Taylor was caught telling a closed-door event in Brisbane of his plans to overhaul the government workforce and get rid of wasteful bureaucracy.

The speech to potential donors at a small-business forum had echoes of the disastrous policy that Peter Dutton took to the 2025 election, which was roundly rejected and which an internal party review found contributed to the massive Labor majority.

It also threatens to derail the ACT Senate campaign of Nick Tyrrell and undermine the Canberra Liberals leader Mark Parton’s efforts to dislodge the Barr Government.

A recording of the speech was obtained by The Canberra Times, which reported that Mr Taylor said there were areas of the public service that could “go immediately” if the Coalition won the next federal election, such as in housing and climate change.

“I’ve been fighting it all my frigging life, and I hate it with a passion … We have agencies across government right now that do not serve the Australian people the way they should. They serve themselves,” he said.

Mr Taylor accused the Albanese Government of “creeping socialism”, warning that “this is how government gets bigger and bigger and bigger”.

In response to questions, Mr Taylor said the Coalition had to take a business-like approach to government.

“The net-zero bureaucracy — gone,” Mr Taylor said. “A housing bureaucracy that’s not delivering another house … Gone. It’s going to go.”

Liberal Senate candidate Nick Tyrrell says Labor is being hypocritical about public service cuts. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

Mr Taylor said he had told “every shadow minister in every area of government” to ”rewrite your orders for every agency, whether it’s the ATO [Australian Taxation Office], whether it’s ASIC [Australian Securities and Investments Commission]”.

“The number-one thing they need to focus on is the national interest, is having an economy that works for Australians, a country that works for Australians,” he said.

“And if a bureaucrat is getting in the way of that, they shouldn’t be there. It’s that simple. This is a business-like approach to government that we desperately need.”

Public Service Minister Katy Gallagher said Mr Taylor’s attacks on the public service confirmed that the Liberals would never change when it came to undermining and politicising the independence of the public service or the party’s plans to sack thousands of government workers.

“They don’t view public servants as workers, they don’t back evidence-based public policy and they will never back Canberra,” she said. ”We know that. We have seen it at every election and the next one will be no different.”

However, Mr Tyrrell said people expected the government and its agencies to be match-fit for the challenges facing the country and the capital.

He said the public service was important to Canberra, but Canberra was more than a public service town.

“Canberrans — public servants, small-business owners, all of us — are suffering under Labor’s low-growth, high-taxing reality,” Mr Tyrrell said.

He said he already had been in to bat for Canberra — on the public service, on the CBD, on the stadium — and would continue to do so publicly and behind the scenes.

“That’s what Canberrans expect, and what they’re not getting from Senator Gallagher,” Mr Tyrrell said.

“Canberrans also deserve more than Senator Gallagher’s tired, well-worn lines and scare campaigns about the APS.

“It was Senator Gallagher and Labor that were exposed by the Independent Parliamentary Budget Office for having plans to cut 41,000 jobs to achieve a budget surplus. I think Canberrans expect answers from Senator Gallagher, not just more deflection and finger-pointing.”

Mr Parton’s office referred Region to his speech to the party’s May Federal Council in Melbourne in which he successfully moved a motion calling on the federal Liberal Party to encourage the public service to pursue excellence and integrity, and to focus on its noble mission of serving the Australian people.

He told the council then that it was easy to demonise Canberra and the public service, but an effective government needed an effective public service.

“This is the moment when you decide whether you want your party to go with either some One Nation-style, cheap political pointscoring, or to be a sensible, constructive party of government,” Mr Parton said.

canberra.title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day does a lot right but is let down by the greater MCU
canberra.snippet: 2026 is the year Marvel chose to return to its biggest hits: the Avengers and Spider-Man. The two franchises combined have brought in ove...
canberra.content:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day is the newest Marvel movie and the first to hit cinemas in 2026. Photo: Sony Pictures.

2026 is the year Marvel chose to return to its biggest hits: the Avengers and Spider-Man.

The two franchises combined have brought in over $10 billion for Marvel, and after a recent lean run in form, it was a surefire way for the studio to bring in some coin.

The first of their two big blockbusters this year is Spider-Man: Brand New Day, the fourth movie starring Tom Holland as the iconic wall-crawler.

Brand New Day is set several years after the events of the previous Spider-Man film, which saw the world forget who Peter Parker is after a spell cast by Dr Strange.

With no one knowing who he is, Peter becomes a recluse, focusing solely on his responsibility as a crime fighter while following his former friends via social media.

Spider-Man has become a popular figure within New York, with even the captain of the local police department calling on him to help reduce crime.

When a mysterious villain who can possess people’s minds and control their actions begins breaking into top-secret government facilities, Spider-Man must locate the telepath and uncover the cover-up they’re trying to expose.

Brand New Day is the first Spider-Man movie in half a decade, which is crazy to think about, as it feels the character has never left the cultural zeitgeist.

It’s always pretty exciting when a new blockbuster comes out, and this one was no different. Thankfully, this new film is quite a bit of fun.

Off the top, this is easily Tom Holland’s best performance in this franchise. Comparing him from his first outing to now is almost night and day. He’s grown as an actor and delivers a great performance as a man struggling with the weight of the world on his shoulders.

Zendaya as MJ, Jon Bernthal as Punisher and Sadie Sink as the mysterious villain are also very strong, all adding emotional weight to what could have been dismissed as ‘just another superhero movie’.

The film’s aesthetic is the best among the newer Spider-Man movies. The first half, especially, feels like scenes ripped from early-2000s Spider-Man comics. It was fantastic.

Mixing these with some very impressive action set pieces made the film’s overall look visually pleasing.

But there are issues, including story beats and how it fits into the greater Marvel Cinematic Universe.

The first half of the film felt almost perfect. It was a street-level crime-fighting movie that spent time with the character we paid to watch.

It was personal and intricate. However, there is a specific point about an hour in, with a cameo from an Avenger, where the movie’s smaller focus shifted to building out the larger world of the Marvel franchise.

It doesn’t completely derail the movie by any means, but the direction it takes from that point isn’t as engaging as the opening act.

Sadie Sink’s character is also a slight point of contention. While the performance is great, people familiar with the source material for her character will be left scratching their heads.

She felt like a massive departure from her comic counterpart and more like a moment for readers to go, ‘Oh damn, I know her!’ in the cinema than as a character necessary for this movie’s plot.

The choice to have Zendaya return is also a mixed bag. Again, she is a true acting powerhouse, but where the narrative left her at the end of the last film, the decision to have her back here felt more like a retread than a push toward the story’s progression.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day is the best of the Tom Holland movies. When it shines, it shines bright, and it truly looks to bring something fresh to the exhausting superhero genre, especially in its first act.

Unfortunately, a handful of story beats do prevent it from reaching its highest potential. Its change of focus led me from thinking, ‘We’re on for the best Spider-Man movie ever’ about an hour in, to ‘Yeah, that was a bit of fun’, by the end.

With all the things the movie does well, there are just as many things it does that left me a tad disappointed.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day is showing in cinemas across the country.

canberra.title: Doing it Tough means getting results, says new minister
canberra.snippet: The ACT’s new cabinet minister aims to live up to her name, but in the nicest possible way. Brindabella MLA Caitlin Tough is as sur...
canberra.content:
New minister Caitlin Tough in her Brindabella heartland. Photos: Ian Bushnell.

The ACT’s new cabinet minister aims to live up to her name, but in the nicest possible way.

Brindabella MLA Caitlin Tough is as surprised as anyone to be elevated to cabinet after less than two years in the Legislative Assembly. That probably contributed to an attack of nerves when Chief Minister Andrew wheeled out the new appointments last week following Yvette Berry’s resignation, although it wasn’t apparent.

Indeed, she is more excited than daunted by the challenges of her new responsibilities, which include the thankless Corrections portfolio, along with Women, Seniors and Veterans; Human Rights; Community Services; and Prevention of Family and Domestic Violence.

Previously a public service policy wonk and advocate for women living with endometriosis, of which she is one, Ms Tough has assiduously been cultivating her electorate as part of the wave of Labor renewal in Brindabella, along with Taimus Werner-Gibbings.

As the mother of a six-year-old, she aligned with the changing demographic in Tuggeranong, which is now attracting young families.

The fruits of her work were clear when we sat down for a chat at a Gordon coffee shop, and several people came over to congratulate her on her new role.

So she already has some political capital to bring into cabinet, where she plans to continue advocating for her electorate as well as for her portfolios.

“Being in the cabinet, everyone’s got to fight for their projects and stand up for their communities and their portfolios,” Ms Tough says

She sees herself as a problem solver – at a policy level and on the ground – and as achieving tangible results, such as new businesses opening at the Richardson shops and the new South Tuggeranong Health Centre.

“I’ve always been a hard worker. I get my feet under the desk, understand what’s going on, and get things through. I’ve had a career where I’ve been able to take a problem and get something to happen,” she says.

“I also love big policy thinking and in previous jobs have been able to have big policy ideas and see them through to fruition.

“I actually want to take the problems from my community and make something happen.”

“I am very, very persistent”: Caitlin Tough is ready to dive into her work and get results.

Ms Tough says she’d prefer to work with people to achieve things, even the opposition, but is unfazed if they don’t.

She is hardly the bulldozer type, but if people think she will be a pushover, think again.

“I think my caucus colleagues and now cabinet colleagues would be able to tell you that when I want something done, I am very, very persistent and keep pointing out why this is a good idea, how it can be done, and come to them with solutions of how we can do it,” she says.

But Ms Tough isn’t about to sound off with policy pronouncements or rattle off a list of things to do just yet.

She plans to get properly briefed and talk to her stakeholders first. However, she has always been about connecting her constituents with the services they may need. She is more than aware of the cost-of-living issues afflicting Canberrans, including the increase in people using food pantries.

But on one subject dear to her heart, she doesn’t hold back: women’s health and employment. She believes there is a lot at stake if there is a change of government both federally and in the ACT in 2028.

She says ACT women have access to better healthcare, including abortion, because of Labor policies.

“We believe that reproductive health is healthcare and are not here to try and change access to it and make it harder in any way,” Ms Tough says.

“A vote for a Liberal government risks losing some of that healthcare access and losing some of that economic opportunity.”

Ms Tough may be Labor through and through and a champion of the south, but she stresses being available for everyone in Canberra.

She knows her portfolios are challenging, but she wants to work with the community to make a difference.

“So my door’s always open to talk to people,” she says.

“I also can’t believe growing up as a girl from the Central Coast that I could ever have made it into being a cabinet minister, so today is a bit surreal still, but I cannot wait to get working on them.”

canberra.title: I held my first dinner party – and only had one panic attack
canberra.snippet: As I lay upon the bathroom floor, trying to cool my sweaty skin and slow my racing heart, I wondered: Am I doing dinner parties wrong? Th...
canberra.content:
At first, I was daunted by the dinner party. But once we got cooking, it basically became a wholesome team-building exercise. Photo: Dave Lastovskiy.

As I lay upon the bathroom floor, trying to cool my sweaty skin and slow my racing heart, I wondered: Am I doing dinner parties wrong?

This was not the sophisticated soiree I’d imagined. Instead I was gripping the granite and monitoring the clock for my guests’ impending arrival, frozen – ironically – by the threat of a fast-defrosting fish.

Once a common occurrence, these days, we don’t often throw dinner parties.

To my memory, somewhere around the mid-90s, everyone simultaneously decided to demolish their dining rooms. Modern home design has largely followed that trend, and I don’t know many people who now have a separate, formal dining space in their homes.

Personally, I’ve developed a vendetta against “open plan living” since having children.

I’m all for supervising the kiddos, but I don’t necessarily need to watch my children watch Bluey. And I definitely don’t always want them to have eyes on me, especially not in the kitchen – where nagging is most prolific, and I’m invariably at my busiest.

Where am I meant to hide? I’ve had to build a walk-in pantry as a sort of panic room.

Nowadays, millennials look upon dinner parties the same way we do ironing, or talking on the phone: No, thank you, that would make me deeply uncomfortable.

But two things happened recently that convinced me it was time for me to hold such a wholesome event.

First, I turned 40. As officially “middle-aged”, it felt only fitting that I – to coin a cringe millennial phrase – “did some adulting”.

Second, we renovated our vintage country kitchen (read: dilapidated Ikea home jobby held together by pavers, chicken wire, a wing and a prayer), replacing it with a Mediterranean-style haven of sprawling storage, oversized benches and modern appliances.

Inspired – and pretty confident my culinary prowess would also be upgraded by osmosis – I issued a few friends with formal invitations for a Mediterranean feast.

A bold move. I have never even been to Mediterranea!

(Calm down, I know that’s Mediterroneous.)

Undeterred by lack of knowledge or experience, I promised my guests a bold headliner: A whole fish.

Now, my sense of humour may be dry – but my fish would not be!

After a singular practice run, with a snapper scarcely bigger than a goldfish, the big day saw my helpful husband bring home a 2.7 kg monstrosity.

“Where do you want it?” he asked.

Suddenly, I realised I had no idea how to store, season or cook this fish. Or any other food. Or set a table. Or speak to people. Or have a birthday.

And so began my slow decline into fish-related insanity and ultimately, a pescatarian panic attack which left me on the bathroom floor, miles from the soothing shores of the Mediterranean or the smug afterglow of a successful dinner party.

I was convinced that middle age would bring me natural wisdom, and that the new kitchen would bring to the surface my previously unseen instinctual culinary skills.

But behind the bravado, it seems my inner-millennial remained resistant.

Fortunately, while I’d clearly bitten off more than I could chew in many regards, I had gotten one key element of the dinner party right. I’d kept my invite list small and manageable (unlike the bloody fish).

Just as I was considering selling my voice to a sea witch in return for fish-related favours, my friends arrived. Voices of reason that they are, they gently lifted me from the depths of despair and brought me back to life.

They also brought sweets, which was nice of them.

I think the reason I’ve always shied away from holding dinner parties is because I’m a prepper. I like to be prepared. I like to cook, clean and get dirty work done in advance, so when guests arrive I am free to focus entirely on my social anxiety.

Behind my bravado, I question my life choices and send up a private prayer to protect my guests from food poisoning. Photo: Hayley Nicholls.

I’m also not as great at multi-tasking as it may appear to the casual observer. You can have good conversation or fine motor skills – not both.

But actually, once the house was full of friends, chatter and laughter, the chaos became part of the fun.

My picture-perfect kitchen quickly disappeared. In its place, surfaces were littered with discarded present-wrapping, used tea towels and stray wine glasses. Dirty dishes piled up sky-high.

And my wildly over-the-top menu – which was so clearly at odds with my actual skill level and number of actual hands – meant that everyone had to pitch in. It was messy, intimate, chaotic, yet somehow relaxed.

And so, I found the beauty of the dinner party: It’s authentic.

Too often we feel pressure to present curated versions of ourselves to the world. The dinner party naturally challenges that. Because this isn’t a restaurant, it’s my home. And I’m not a chef, I’m just your friend, asking you to join me for dinner.

And to take a leap of faith on this fish with me.

canberra.title: Satire leads to Questacon’s real push to attract global music sensation
canberra.snippet: A satirical article in The Betoota Advocate, mocking the announcement of music sensation Raye as the headlining act for the Canberra leg ...
canberra.content:
An article in the satirical publication The Betoota Advocate has prompted Questacon to make a concerted push to host music sensation Raye. Photo: James Coleman/Insert: Aliyah Otchere.

A satirical article in The Betoota Advocate, mocking the announcement of music sensation Raye as the headlining act for the Canberra leg of the Spilt Milk festival, has prompted Questacon to make a real push to host the pop artist.

Raye, best known for her song ‘Where is my husband!’, averages over 43 million monthly listeners on Spotify, with her top song amassing over 1.3 billion streams on the platform.

Raye was announced as the headliner for Spilt Milk last week alongside Lewis Capaldi, whose song ‘Someone You Loved’ has over 4.39 billion streams.

The article mockingly stated the only reason Raye agreed to headline this year’s festival was that she was offered a private tour of the popular science centre.

“It’s always been a bucket list item for me,” ‘Raye’ supposedly said to Betoota.

“So when they told me they could roll it into the Canberra show, it was a no-brainer.

“Lewis (Capaldi) is apparently also keen, so it should be a bit of fun,” laughed the popular singer about another huge name on the lineup.

Upon the article’s release, Questacon responded to the publication’s satirical claims and, in turn, made a genuine offer to the artist.

“Although The Betoota Advocate is famous for satire, we figured there’s no harm in discussing what a visit from Raye could look like,” Questacon posted to its socials.

“Do you think she has a favourite element?’ We asked ourselves. “We then guessed ‘probably carbon.’

“This is because we heard her mention, ‘I would like a ring, I would like a ring, I would like a diamond ring on my wedding finger, I would like a big and shiny diamond, diamond, diamond, diamond’.

“As you may know, diamonds are around 99.95% carbon. We would gladly welcome other artists from the Spilt Milk 2026 lineup.”

Despite Questacon’s similarly tongue-in-cheek response to Beetoota, Executive Director of Questacon Jo White took the time to formally offer the popstar a legitimate tour of the centre while also offering free entry to any of the performers of this year’s music festival.

“Canberra comes alive during events like Spilt Milk, and we wanted to join in the excitement in a uniquely Questacon way,” Ms White said.

“After seeing The Betoota Advocate‘s playful suggestion that Raye had agreed to perform because of a promised visit to Questacon, we thought we’d embrace the joke and extend the invitation ourselves.

“Questacon is Australia’s National Science and Technology Centre, and we welcome half a million visitors each year. Whether you are a local or a visitor, here for a music festival, a holiday, or a school trip, there’s something for everyone to discover at Questacon.

“We’d be thrilled to host any of the artists performing at Spilt Milk, but we’re equally excited to welcome the festival-goers who will be visiting Canberra in December.”

Spilt Milk will be held at the Exhibition Park on Saturday 12 December. Tickets are available now.

Questacon is open 9 am to 5 pm daily.

australia.title: Queensland reveals concept plans for Brisbane Olympic stadium precinct – but critics say they are ‘fantasy vision’
australia.snippet: David Crisafulli says ‘Queenslanders will enjoy for generations’ as opponents point to lack of detail Get our breaking news email , free ...
australia.content:
The Queensland government has released new concept images for a parkland precinct to surround the 2032 Olympic stadium, as it seeks to quell concern at the loss of Brisbane’s largest inner-city parkland.

But opponents of the plans – now entering the early construction phase – to build a stadium at Brisbane’s Victoria Park say the concept images are a “fantasy vision” with no detail, and which overlook the likely need for carparks, roads, transport links and plazas to accommodate large crowds.

The government says its plan will retain two-thirds of Victoria Park as green space, after the construction of an oval-shaped 63,000-seat stadium, and a new national aquatic centre.

The draft precinct plan and concept images show two pedestrian bridges, built over the Brisbane inner-city bypass, a road which severs most of the parkland site from Spring Hill and the Brisbane CBD.

It also proposes flooding space occupied by football fields to expand the York’s Hollow wetland at the site, and building a public amphitheatre near the stadium.

“This state-shaping precinct is about legacy – unlocking a world-class free precinct that Queenslanders will enjoy for generations, long after the flame is extinguished,” the premier, David Crisafulli, said on Sunday.

“Just as South Bank defined a city as the gift for Expo ‘88, Victoria Park will be the legacy of 2032 – a place that belongs to Queenslanders once the games have gone.”

The government’s draft legacy plan emphasised the retention of green space and that Victoria Park would be more accessible than it is today.

The heritage-listed parkland, known as Barrambin by traditional owners, has been a controversial choice as the main stadium for the 2032 Olympics. It has long been underutilised and hosted a golf course until a few years ago.

In addition to local concerns about the loss of parkland, and concerns by First Nations people about damage to a culturally significant site, Victoria Park also comes with logistical and geographical issues.

Critics of the state’s plans said the plans appeared only designed to present a “fantasy vision” of how the park might be redeveloped, but that these seemed not to take several factors into account.

Save Victoria Park spokesperson Sue Bremner said the “misleading” impressions were an attempt to distract from Olympics budget blowouts.

“We have said time and time again – it is one of the most complex, expensive and poorly connected sites in Brisbane to build sporting venues,” Bremner said.

“What we saw today was not a plan. It was another insulting fantasy vision with no details.

“Where are the car parks? Where are the roads? Where’s the connection to the train station? Where are the crowd-holding plazas? The ramp from the [bypass]?”

“The time for empty slogans, greenwashed architect impressions and budget lowballing is over.”

australia.title: EVs and hybrids approach half of Australian new car sales amid ongoing fuel crisis
australia.snippet: Australians bought EVs and hybrids at nearly same rate as petrol cars between April and June, Australian Automobile Association data show...
australia.content:
Australians are now buying electric and hybrid vehicles at the same rate as traditional petrol-powered cars, according to new data that shows EV sales doubled in the months after the peak of the fuel price spike.

Fuel prices are again on track to top $2 a litre, after the federal government’s fuel excise reductions – introduced to offset the impact of the ongoing crisis in the Middle East – come to an end on Sunday.

The Australian Automobile Association (AAA) has released its latest EV Index, showing motorists pivoting to electric and hybrid options in the three months from April to June, coinciding with the period of instability in fuel prices.

Almost half of sales of new cars from that period were electric, plug-in hybrid or hybrid vehicles.

The market share of EVs (21.03%) and plug-in hybrids (10.58%) were both records.

Fuel prices peaked in March, amid instability in the Middle East that affected key supply routes.

The federal government intervened on 30 March, announcing a fuel excise reduction that has provided some relief at the bowser.

The AAA’s figures show that sales of battery electric vehicles more than doubled in the second quarter of 2026 – up from from 34,435 in the first three months, to 69,414 between April and June.

The AAA says the increase is the largest-ever quarterly rise for electric vehicles.

Hybrid sales were also at an all-time high, but were overtaken by the surge in motorists purchasing EVs.

Sales of traditional internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles fell from 64.23% in the first quarter to 2026 to 50.84% in the most-recent data. It is the lowest-ever market share for petrol-powered vehicles and their biggest-ever quarterly drop, the AAA says.

When the AAA’s EV index began recording data in 2022, ICE cars accounted for nine out of ever 10 sold.

australia.title: Concept images of controversial 2032 Brisbane Olympics precinct revealed – as it happened
australia.snippet: Community members concerned about loss of community green space and areas of cultural importance. This blog is now closed Get our breakin...
australia.content:
What we learned: Sunday, 2 August

Kat Wong

That’s where we’ll leave the blog for today. We’ll be back tomorrow morning, but for now, enjoy the rest of your weekend.

Here are today’s top news stories:

  • The deputy opposition leader, Jane Hume, told Insiders the prime minister had shown an “extraordinary lack of curiosity” on alleged corruption at construction sites as she backed calls for a Senate inquiry into the matter.

  • Australia has been warned a deadly strain of bird flu is “starting to take off” after more than 80 dead and sick birds were found at an island in South Australia.

  • The health minister, Mark Butler, rejected calls for the prime minister to stand down his special envoy for defence, veterans’ affairs and northern Australia, Luke Gosling, who was charged over an alleged assault on the Northern Territory’s administrator.

  • Six children in the Philippines have been removed from harm as a 74-year-old West Australian man was sentenced to 10 years in jail after pleading guilty to online child abuse material offences.

  • The Queensland government has unveiled concept images of the controversial Victoria Park precinct ahead of the 2032 Brisbane Olympics.

Key events

  • 8h ago

    What we learned: Sunday, 2 August

  • 9h ago

    Concept images of controversial Victoria Park precinct revealed ahead of 2032 Brisbane Olympics

  • 9h ago

    ‘Starting to take off’: bird flu mass mortality likely

  • 11h ago

    Land rights ‘coming home’ as Yolngu leaders launch landowners’ council at Garma festival

  • 11h ago

    Icac should be ‘free of political interference’, deputy opposition leader says

  • 11h ago

    Jane Hume says PM shown ‘extraordinary lack of curiosity’ on alleged corruption on construction sites

  • 12h ago

    Aged-care nurses get pay increase

  • 12h ago

    Good morning

Australian man jailed over child abuse material as children removed from harm

Six children have been removed from harm in the Philippines as a West Australian man was sentenced to a maximum of 10 years and six months in prison for online child abuse material offences.

Australian Border Force officers found videos of children being sexually abused on the 74-year-old man’s mobile phone after selecting him for a baggage examination after he arrived at Perth Airport in May 2025.

As the Australian Federal Police examined his phone, they found conversations between him and a woman in the Philippines where she transmitted child abuse material.

The matter was later referred to the Philippine Internet Crimes Against Children Centre, and the Philippine National Bureau of Investigation Human Trafficking Division began an investigation.

In April 2026. the division executed a search warrant at a home in Bislig City, Philippines, where a woman was arrested and six children, who were known to her, were removed from harm.

The 32-year-old woman was later charged and is before the court in the Philippines.

The 74-year-old man was sentenced at Perth District Court after pleading guilty to a series of charges including three counts of using a carriage service to groom another person to make it easier to procure persons under 16.

ABF superintendent John Eldridge said:

Unfortunately, we are finding child abuse material on digital devices of travellers all too often, but when we do, we act decisively with our law enforcement partners to ensure these perpetrators face criminal charges and prevent further harm.

NSW premier says evidence must come before judgment following Icac hearings

As the NSW anti-corruption watchdog investigates allegations of corruption against people associated with the state’s Liberal branch, the premier, Chris Minns has said Icac must be able to present its evidence free from political commentary.

We need the evidence to be accumulated before we pass a judgment on it, and that’s really Icac’s job.

What’s interesting and perhaps worrying inquiry for me is that over the same time that this inquiry has been taking place, One Nation’s vote has skyrocketed, and they’ve got nothing to do with this Icac investigation.

My concern is that people say, “Well, I’ve seen Labor at Icac, and I’ve seen the Liberal Party at Icac. I’m going to vote for a third party this time.”

So, I don’t think it’s necessarily the big boon for our political party that many believe, and I also think it’s sad for politics when people who are in elected positions are acting in this way because it casts a pall over everybody in politics.

Ben Smee

Continuing on from last post ….

Opponents of the proposal have long scoffed at claims that most of the parkland surrounding a new 60,000-seat stadium will remain valuable green space.

Save Victoria Park spokesperson Sue Bremner said the “misleading” impressions were an attempt to distract from Olympics budget blowouts.

We have said time and time again – it is one of the most complex, expensive and poorly connected sites in Brisbane to build sporting venues.

What we saw today was not a plan. It was another insulting fantasy vision with no details. Where are the car parks? Where are the roads? Where’s the connection to the train station? Where are the crowd-holding plazas? The ramp from the [bypass]?

Concept images of controversial Victoria Park precinct revealed ahead of 2032 Brisbane Olympics

Ben Smee

The Queensland government has released new concept images showing Brisbane’s broader Victoria Park precinct after the construction of the 2032 Olympic stadium and aquatic centre.

Victoria Park is Brisbane’s largest inner-city parkland and a site of significance for First Nations elders.

It is a controversial choice as home to Brisbane’s upcoming Olympics, leading to protests from community members concerned about the loss of community green space and areas of cultural importance.

The images – along with a master plan for the broader parkland site – show plans for two new pedestrian bridges across the inner-city bypass. The road severs the site from Spring Hill and the rest of the Brisbane CBD and had been a significant constraint for planners.

It also proposes flooding existing sports fields on the site to expand the York’s Hollow wetland.

The government says the precinct will “become a world-class destination that celebrates Brisbane’s unique outdoor lifestyle while creating a vibrant place where people can gather, play, connect and experience unforgettable moments for generations to come”.

It says about two-thirds of the existing park will remain public green space.

‘Starting to take off’: bird flu mass mortality likely

A mass mortality event, potentially triggered by bird flu, mirrors what’s happened as the deadly disease spread overseas, environmental advocates warn.

AAP reports, more than 80 dead and sick greater crested terns have been found at an island called Baudin Rock in South Australia.

Authorities say it is likely to be the first mass mortality event from the deadly disease.

The Invasive Species Council’s chief executive, Jack Gough, said Australia was still at the very early stages of the H5 outbreak, but it could spread quickly.

It seems the virus is starting to take off, mirroring the experience in South America.

[That is:] early detections, then rapid increases in numbers and spread, leading to mass mortality events in wildlife.

Bird flu has caused significant illness and deaths in poultry, wild birds and mammals in Asia; Europe; North and South America; and the Arctic and Antarctic, according to Wildlife Health Australia.

Over 600 bird species and more than 100 mammalian species, including wild marine and land mammals, have been affected.

‘More than just objects’: Australian booksellers raise alarm over ‘horrific’ destruction of rare titles to feed AI

Vendors and rare books experts are increasingly worried that these artefacts may be under threat of destruction by generative AI companies seeking to feed their ravenous technology with new texts.

Stephanie Convery writes the fears stem from a copyright lawsuit brought against AI company Anthropic in the United States by book authors. Unsealed court files revealed earlier this year that the company was engaging in the practice of “destructive scanning” – buying physical books, slicing off the spines to more efficiently scan the pages, then pulping the remains – and had sought to keep it quiet. The judge ruled this was lawful under US copyright law, as it amounted to “transformative use”.

The practice is now understood to be widespread among generative AI companies, and recent reports suggest intermediaries are stepping up to facilitate the process.

Australian secondhand booksellers are wondering if they have been caught up in the AI supply chain after they recently experienced waves of orders that did not fit with usual customer patterns.

Nation-first fully integrated bionic arm to hit shelves

A university startup has developed Australia’s first fully integrated bionic arm, giving hope to users who have given up on heavy, painful prosthetics, AAP reports.

Cost, weight and accessibility changes means 35–40% of prosthetic users in high-income countries end up rejecting their devices.

But after speaking to dozens of people with limb difference to identify key challenges over 10 years of development, University of Melbourne-led startup Meablex have developed a bionic arm that could change the experience of prosthetics for users.

It features soft and flexible materials that weigh about half what a conventional prosthetic does.

It’s also been designed with an adjustable socket to make the prosthetic easier to fit, and is more reliable to control than others currently on the market.

Senior research engineer Dr Alireza Mohammadi told AAP:

Our technology combines a lightweight 3D-printed prosthetic hand with a new sensorised socket that detects subtle muscle movement, rather than relying only on traditional electrical muscle signals.

He hopes the device can enter the market next year, following clinical trials and regulatory approvals later this year.

We’re not just looking at Australia, we are thinking more globally.

It will definitely affect many lives and many people that can use this device.

How a tragedy in a homeless camp laid bare regional Australia’s housing crisis

Three months ago, a homeless encampment in Wagga Wagga made headlines when a newborn baby died at a nearby riverbank after their mother gave birth in a tent.

Since then, the response to the growing crisis has been fractured and confusing and the community is divided on how to manage the camp.

Some have jumped in to help, while others have sided with the council in calls to clear it out.

Cait Kelly writes about the ways the housing crisis is playing out in regional Australia.

PM urged to stand aside special envoy after assault charge

The deputy opposition leader, Jane Hume, has called on the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, to take action against his special envoy for defence, veterans’ affairs and northern Australia, Luke Gosling.

The MP has been charged over an alleged assault on the Northern Territory’s administrator earlier this month.

Hume told ABC’s Insiders it was a “pretty serious charge”.

It’s alleged at this stage but the charge has been laid.

Anthony Albanese has been very quick to condemn other people and request, in previous lives, that prime ministers stand down their ministers or their senior members of parliament for far less.

I think that he should live up to his own high expectations and stand Luke Gosling down.

Gosling previously said he could not comment as the matter was before the courts, but thanked his family and vowed to work to serve his constituents.

Penny Wong addresses Garma festival: ‘We are not a monoculture and we have never been’

The announcement was delivered before a powerful audience that included senior cabinet ministers Penny Wong, Malarndirri McCarthy and Jason Clare, and Pacific leaders including Timor-Leste’s prime minister, Kay Rala Xanana Gusmão.

As the ripples of the announcement spread across Garma, AAP reports, Wong used her address to draw a contrast with those she suggested were trying to divide Australians.

At a time when there are those who seek to set us apart, First Nations peoples, with your generosity, remind us our many different stories brought together make us stronger.

We are not a monoculture and we have never been.

Continuing on from last post …

Djawa Yunupingu, leader of the Yothu Yindi Foundation, tied the new council directly to Yolngu law, ancestral obligation and an unbroken connection to Country, and said Yolngu wanted development and opportunity in a way that kept control on Country and in the hands of traditional owners.

We have tourism at Bawaka and Banubanu and it is my dream that there will be a five-star resort on this beautiful Country.

We have schools that are teaching our young people. We have a Garma Institute that will be our own university and it will hold our knowledge right here.

He said the Yolngu people knew every inch of their Country and the council would stand ready to work alongside the army, the navy and the air force to defend it.

It will work with the government and with mining companies, any company who wants to do business with us.

It will work in partnership with the Northern Land Council for the people. We will be a part of the economic life of this nation whilst never losing who we are and what we stand for.

Yunupingu thanked the Northern Land Council and its chair, Matthew Ryan, for protecting Yolngu interests and standing with them as they prepared for the transition, AAP reports.
